pr_title: Limit the number of concurrently opened indexes
pr_body:
# Pull Request

## Related issue
Relevant to #1841, fixes #3382

## What does this PR do?

### User standpoint

- Limit the number of concurrently opened indexes (currently, the number of indexes that can be concurrently opened is computed at startup)
- When too many an index is opened, the least recently used one is closed and its virtual memory released.
- This allows a user to have an arbitrary number of indexes of an arbitrary size

### Implementation standpoint

- Added a LRU cache map in `index-scheduler::lru`. A more complete implementation  (eg with helper functions not used here) is available but would better fit a dedicated crate.
- Use the LRU cache map in the `IndexScheduler`. To simplify the lifecycle of indexes, they are never removed from the cache when they are in the middle of a resize or delete operation. To achieve this, an intermediate `Vec` stores the UUIDs of the indexes that are in the middle of such an operation.
- Upon creating the index scheduler object, compute the total virtual memory that is adressable by using a dichotomic search on the max size of an index. Use this as a base to compute the number of indexes that can be open with 2TiB per index. If the virtual memory address space is lower than 2TiB, then only allow for 1 index of a fraction of that size.
pr_comments: I feel like with the tests I did, this PR is now ready for review.

- Change default index size to 10GiB
- Default to 100 concurrent indexes in Unixes, 10 in Windows

Added an update with the following:

- We compute an "index budget" when the Index scheduler is created, to know how much cumulated virtual memory we can allocate through memmap before exhausting the virtual address space. A fraction of the budget is then split to determine how many indexes can be opened simultaneously in the cache with a size of 2TiB. If that number is 0, then there can be only one index in the cache with a size of whatever budget is available.
- As computing the budget adds 2 seconds at startup, it is disabled in tests.

This should result in the following:

- No more performance hit due to index resize, except for users with indexes bigger than 2 TiB (if this impedes your use case, please contact us)
- Much lower risk of filling the entirety of the cache
- Adapts to machines with smaller virtual memory address space

I will do a second prototype with these changes soon.

---

### remaining TODO

- Some comments on the PR left unaddressed
- "Invasive" logs that are good for the prototype but should be removed before merging
- Handle the methods that attempt to open all indexes at once
- Check that the added dynamic budget computation doesn't impede usage for Cloud

Pushed an update that handles the methods that attempt to open all indexes at once.

There is now a `try_for_each_index` method that allows to iterate on all indexes. For callers that only needed the names, there is also a new `index_names` method that doesn't open the indexes at all.

The `stats`, `indexes`, `dumps` routes as well as snapshot creation/import and dump import seem to be fixed by this change.  
 
---

There is some performance effect to calling `stats` on a meilisearch with 1000+ indexes: about 8s on Mac (0.8s for 100 indexes, unnoticeable for 10 indexes), about 0.5s on Linux (unnoticeable for 100 indexes or below). I cannot compare with v1 because we couldn't have more than 200 indexes there so the stats route would fail. Interestingly on mac the time for the route to answer decreases when limiting the total virtual memory with `ulimit`. Possibly the allocator is simply slow for big allocations, whereas Linux' is very fast by comparison on that use case.

TODO:

- [x] It appears that indexes are not being registered correctly as `BeingDeleted` currently, this needs checking
- [x] Rebase on `main`
- [x] Squash redundant commits

Follow-ups for subsequent PRs (to be added in the tracking issue and/or opened as different issues):

- Increased Windows/macOS startup time. This could be mitigated by first trying a budget value that should be "good enough" and skipping the dichotomy if it passes.
- Degraded stats performance. This could be mitigated by caching the stats of indexes (eg in the tasks db).
- Finer-grained error handling in the dichotomy: make a difference between allocation errors (continue the dichotomy after marking this value as "bad") and other kinds of errors (stop the dichotomy and report the error to the caller)

Thank you for the review @Kerollmops!

issue_context.title: Don't limit the number or size of indexes
issue_context.body:
## Context

- There is currently an inherent tradeoff between the number of opened indexes and their max size. In v1.0.0, this tradeoff is "fixed" due to the removal of the `--max-index-size` option. We would like to not expose this tradeoff to end users anymore.
- For more context: https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch/discussions/3280
- Also related to issue https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch/issues/1841 that's already planned for the v1.1 milestone

## Implementation

- Automatically resize indexes: this allows to start with a lower "`--max-index-size`" and plan accordingly to the actual space needs of the index.
- Limit the concurrent number of opened indexes: this ensures that we can reach bigger `--max-index-size` by closing least recently used indexes.

I have some draft PRs implementing both of these: https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch/pull/3319 and https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch/pull/3331 

## Specification

A specification PR was opened: see https://github.com/meilisearch/specifications/pull/226
comments: I add the `missing spec` label in case we would need to update the spec. @gmourier and @dureuill
Also this issue could interest @meilisearch/docs-team  regarding the limitations of the search engine

Just discussed with @dureuill, he confirmed the newly introduced limits will be present in the spec, or at least in this issue.
In Linux, only the size of the disk will be the limit (can be different on Windows), so no defined limit of number of indexes 😊

After discussing with @Kerollmops, here are some points that are still to be done after #3331 : 

- [ ] Check that the lock cannot become poisoned due to an *impromptu* panic
- [ ] There is a `indexes` method on the `IndexMapper` and the `Indexer` that return a vector of handles to all the indexes, resulting in all indexes being opened. This is used in several places, such as the API keys, the stats route, and so on.  This results in a failure is the sum of all indexes cannot fit in the virtual memory address space. Several solutions can possibly address this issue:
  1. Have the `indexes` methods return an iterator instead => doesn't prevent caller from `collect`'ng it
  2. Have the `indexes` methods accept a closure with an IndexHandle that cannot be cloned or escape the closure as argument.
  3. Replace the `indexes` methods by `index_stats` methods that return a Vec of stats => not necessarily sufficient for dumps
  4. Wrap the `Index` object in a `LazyIndex` object that doesn't keep the `Index` handle, but reopen it as necessary => Would make sure that the issue cannot popup whatever what the `IndexMapper` clients do, but is very invasive.

For the first iteration, it would be good to at least document the issue in the concerned function, and at least explore option (2) or (3)

Indexing performance concern:

As we have to wait for the indexing task to fail when indexing, if the indexed data is big, we might resize the index multiple times, and so attempt the task multiple times.

This can make indexing bigger datasets much slower, as we would have to attempt indexing them many more times. Two consecutive resizes would result in about tripling the indexing time.

---

Possible solutions discussed with @Kerollmops and @ManyTheFish : 


### 1. Allocate a significant portion of the memory space for the index that is being written to.

- Advantage: No resize for that index
- Cons: the index must be closed to write to another index, losing data locality and having readers wait while the index is being closed. This can be particularly bad in patterns where multiple indexes are updated together with small, incremental updates. 

### 2. Evaluate our process "virtual address space" budget, then allocate it up to some size in the LRU

- Advantage: No special "index being written to" status, limits the need for closing index, improves data locality
- Cons: Will need fine-tuning to avoid situations where the maximum index size is too small, and situations where the budget is taken entirely (due to an index resizing unexpectedly, etc)
- Cons: Having each index be e.g. 2TB (so about 30 indexes if taking half of the available space in linux) will penalize people that have many small indexes.
- Cons: determining the budget takes up to 2 seconds which might slow down startup/first search by that duration

### 3. Choose some "reasonable default" for index size, leave resize a costly operation that should happen infrequently in normal use

- eg 200 GB. Possibly downsize the index for users that have a very small virtual memory index space if opening the index fails.

- Pros: Simple, no need to compute a budget
- Cons: Penalizes people with a few big indexes, as they will suffer resizes.


---

There are 2 use cases to consider:

1. Dump import / first indexation. In this use case, the final size of the index is completely unknown (although we could have the size of the index on size as of the dump creation stored in the dump for a hint)
2. Index update: While the final size of the index is fundamentally unknown, there's a good likelihood that it will remain close to the original size of the index


---

From all this, a first strategy could be:

1. At startup, compute "virtual address space" budget by attempting to open an environment with various sizes dichotomically.
2. Keep a fraction (e.g. 1/2) of this budget as the "index budget".
3. Initialize the LRU to accommodate for N indexes of 1TB of map_size such that the "index budget" is entirely taken. N=6 on Windows, N=50 on Linux/macOS.
4. If the "index budget" is < 1TB, then have a LRU of 1 index with the map_size the entire index budget.

The strategy favors users with a few bigger indexes, as users with many indexes (1000) will have them closed/opened often. OTOH, with many indexes they are probably small, so reading them from disk isn't that much a penalty with a SSD. Moreover, other system limits like simultaneous file handle available to a process (256 on stock Unix) might come into play anyway for keeping many indexes open.

Having an index need more than 1TB of map_size might result in allocation errors if the cache is full. Disregarding Windows this would be a use case with many big indexes or 1 big indexes and many small indexes. This use case could be better handled by making the cache "understand" how much budget it has and how much budget an index takes.

A more recent prototype is available, [see my other message below](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch/issues/3382#issuecomment-1436523578)

--- 

A prototype that removes the restriction on the number or size of indexes is available!

### How to get the prototype?

- Using docker, use the following command: `docker run -p 7700:7700 -v $(pwd)/meili_data:/meili_data getmeili/meilisearch:prototype-unlimited-indexes-0`
- From source, compile Meilisearch on the `prototype-unlimited-indexes-0` tag

### How to use the prototype?

Use the prototype as you would use a `v1.0.0` Meilisearch instance, in particular it is not needed to reindex your data. The prototype should allow you to create as many indexes as wanted, of any arbitrary size (that fits on disk!)

⚠️ Do not use the prototype in production ⚠️

### Use cases we might want to test with the prototype

1. Having one, or a few, big indexes, like >500GiB in size. For this use case it would be interesting to index the data with the prototype to see if there are any significant performance hit compared with e.g. `v0.30` (see performance concern in the [comment above](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch/issues/3382#issuecomment-1429965088))
2. Having many smaller indexes, like >200 indexes. For this use case it would be interesting to perform searches on the various indexes depending on actual workloads, to see if there are any significant performance hit compared with e.g. `v0.30`.

Thanks to anyone taking the time to test this prototype ♥️

Good news, we reached a good first level in preparation for v1.1 RC0 :tada:.

However, I'm reopening this issue because we have some follow-ups that should be addressed before closing:

- Increased Windows/macOS startup time. This could be mitigated by first trying a budget value that should be "good enough" and skipping the dichotomy if it passes.
- Degraded stats performance. This could be mitigated by caching the stats of indexes (eg in the tasks db).
- Finer-grained error handling in the dichotomy: make a difference between allocation errors (continue the dichotomy after marking this value as "bad") and other kinds of errors (stop the dichotomy and report the error to the caller)

So I'm not sure how to best express this and *where in the specification this should appear*, but following the changes made for v1.1, the current status, relevant to the docs team in particular, is the following: 

- Meilisearch can accommodate an **arbitrary number** of indexes as long as the disk size they take is under 2TiB.
- If having indexes bigger in size than 2TiB, then Meilisearch can still accommodate them as long as the sum of the disk sizes taken by any group of 20 of the existing indexes is below 80 TiB (consider that a 100TB SSD was $40,000 in 2020).
- While indexes bigger in size than 2TiB are supported, performance of making updates to these big indexes might be reduced. Feel free to contact us if this impacts your use case.
- While Meilisearch supports an arbitrary number of indexes, having hundreds of indexes accessed at random will trigger more reads from disk and might be slower, so limit the number of concurrently accessed indexes if possible. For instance, if requiring multi-tenancy, consider using tenant tokens in a single index rather than creating one index per tenant.

Cc @gmourier where in the specs do you think it would be best for this to appear?

Discussed with gmourier and opened the following specification PR: https://github.com/meilisearch/specifications/pull/226

Issue description and labels are up to date

review_comments: What I find funny is that we always ask users to `ulimit -Sn 8000` in order to index a large number of documents.
You should probably return an error here if it is not due to an index memory map size issue.
Do you want to wrap here or crash instead? Wouldn't it be better to unwrap?

well like documented the situation is probably impossible, so I don't have a strong opinion either way. The advantage of the wrapping_add is that we don't pollute the branch predictor with one branch we'll never take, but I recon that's a bit of a micro-optimization

I can change if you feel we could use the additional caution

I wanted to propose you use a generic "popular" crate to do this dichotomic search (and avoid logic mistakes), but I am astonished that [no single crate contains the word `dichotomic` at all](https://lib.rs/search?q=dichotomic) 😱
Yes, because they're removed from the db before the deletion starts.
Shouldn't you check for the specific memory mapping error here and return other potential errors for real?

Unfortunately this is not easy to do.

- The dichotomic routine is not written to take into account the possibility of error, although we could change it at the cost of increased complexity
- More annoyingly, while unices are rather well-behaved and will return an OS error 12 when unable to allocate, Windows returns up to 4 different errors, making for a total of 5 cases to handle. I think it is best handled in a follow-up PR.

Looking at various scenarios that can happen here:

1. There is a persistent error wrt to opening the task db that is never resolved. In that case, we will fail opening the task db afterwards and get the error at that point.
2. There is a transient error that is resolved after computing the budget, but before opening the task db. In that case the returned budget will be 0 (1 index of 0 bytes, and the task_db_size will be computed to 0), which will attempt to open the indexes to their "natural size" (or the default size in lmdb if creating the index). This will probably render the instance unusable though as the task db will be MDB_MAP_FULL very early. A restart will be necessary.
3. There is a transient error that is resolved while computing the budget: the budget will be lower than it should be. How much of an issue this poses is dependent on when the issue is resolved. The closer we get to 0 budget, the closer to solution (2) we get.
4. There is a transient error that appear after computing the budget: in that case the budget might not be actual anymore and we'll see allocation errors pop when opening indexes. I try to mitigate that case by taking a fraction of the budget (because the budget is shared with all allocations in the application and can suffer from memory fragmentation), but ultimately this PR cannot address the possible issues caused by e.g. a different part of the programming memory mapping with a big size or making big allocations.

I'll update the PR to comment at least on the "persistent error" scenario, which looks the most likely to me.
Thank you very much @dureuill, for this explanation. You can also link to this GitHub comment if the reader needs more info 😃

Apologies, I see my doc comment was insufficient, and I had to think again what the full reason was.

The reason is performance.

min_by_key gives us a shared reference to the generation, which is an atomic integer. Atomic integers require an atomic load with an implicit memory fence to be correct. It is unnecessary because we have an exclusive reference, meaning either we have a single thread or we have some kind of lock that handled the memory fencing for us.

This is why atomic integers allow direct access "as if they were simple integers" when we can provide an exclusive reference to them. Which is what I use here.

Alternatively, I could have:

- performed loads with an acquire semantics, but that would be subefficient performance wise
- performed loads with a relaxed semantics, and put a an explicit memory fence above the loop, but even this fence is unnecessary
- performed loads with a relaxed semantics, and put a comment explaining why this is not a problem.

I preferred shunting completely the atomic load by using the `get_mut()` method that returns a exclusive reference to the atomic.

To be clear, here the important semantic distinction is exclusivity, not mutability of the `&mut`.

Feel free to tell me if:

1. the explanation is clearer now
2. if you prefer that I change for one of alternatives outlined above
3. how you'd like me to improve the doc comment so the reason becomes clearer. It could also be a module wide comment because I'm using the exclusiveness of `&mut AtomicU64` in quite a few locations.
Thank you very much. Much better!
I hope we will release the crate in the near future, just to avoid having to maintain this file in the repository :)
Yep I'll talk about that during pre-release I think
